# Trellis Guide

The language-neutral guide for services, apps, agents, and devices that consume
Trellis. Read it with the [TypeScript](llms-typescript.txt), [Rust](llms-rust.txt),
or [Svelte](llms-svelte.txt) guide, from the same release or checkout as the CLI
and libraries.

## Overview

Trellis provides authenticated, contract-defined communication and runtime
resources for TypeScript and Rust participants. Native IDL generates each
participant's typed API. Connected calls run over NATS; the libraries own
bootstrap, proofs, authorization, and connection lifecycle.

Trellis owns native contract compilation, generated APIs, authenticated
communication, connection lifecycle, and declared runtime resources. It does not
choose an application's configuration format, environment parser, database, ORM,
dependency injection, folder structure, UI framework, or testing policy.
Application-owned code can use other systems alongside Trellis. The requirements
in these guides apply when using Trellis surfaces: a Trellis event's proof and
subject are runtime-owned, but an application may use a separate message system
for unrelated work. Examples choose a concrete stack to demonstrate Trellis, not
to require that stack.

Use documentation from the same Trellis release or source revision as the
installed libraries and CLI. In a checkout these files live under `docs/static/`;
the raw GitHub links address the main branch and may be newer than an installed
release. Use matching runtime, SDK, and generated package versions.

This unreleased Revision 7 branch implements authoritative Auth capability
evaluation, reviewed catalog acceptance, logical authorization sessions, signed
verification material, and durable retirement effects. OAuth/Callout admission
and SDK/provider transports use this model. The former GrantBinding/browser-bind
protocols are not a compatibility option; do not adapt applications to them or
install a watcher per context as a fallback.

Consumer AGENTS templates are available under `templates/`. They describe the
Trellis boundary; application policies belong in the consumer repository.

Human guides on the docs site: `/guides/write-a-service` (service walkthrough),
`/guides/authoring-contracts` (IDL), `/guides/testing-trellis-services`,
`/guides/install-trellis` and `/guides/running-trellis/development`,
`/guides/running-trellis/binaries` and `/guides/running-trellis/podman`
(installing and running Trellis), and `/api` (public language
APIs). Generated participant source defines the exact names available for a
project's declared actions.

## Project And Generation

The workflow:

1. Author the `.trellis` files explicitly listed by `[sources]`.
2. Set `[package]`, `[dependencies]`, and language outputs in `trellis.toml`;
   run `trellis update` to resolve changes into `trellis.lock`.
3. Run `trellis install` to reproduce locked dependencies and `trellis generate`
   after IDL edits; it re-records your own package in `trellis.lock` (commit
   it), and `trellis generate --check` fails on a stale lock or output in CI.
   `trellis generate --watch` supports the edit loop.
4. Depend on the one ordinary generated package for your language. Import its
   `apis`, `participants`, and `apps` namespaces, not separate API or participant
   packages.
5. Connect through that participant's supported runtime API. Use generated calls
   and resolved resource handles; do not reconstruct Trellis transport metadata.

A minimal `trellis.toml` is:

```toml
[package]
name = "orders-trellis"
workspace = "ghcr.io/acme"
version = "1.0.0"

[sources]
orders = "contract.trellis"
```

### Workspaces and IDs

A package's workspace is the registry location it is published from, a
lower-case registry host and repository path such as `ghcr.io/acme` or
`localhost:5000/dev`. Workspace and name are its full identity,
`ghcr.io/acme/orders-trellis`, which is also its repository. Whoever can push
there owns the names under it, so two communities can each publish a package
named `orders-trellis`. A package without `workspace` gets `localhost`: it can
be a path dependency, installed from source, and used in tests, but never
published, and a published package cannot depend on it. Declare the workspace
from the start for anything you will publish; changing it later is a new
package with new IDs and needs a new deployment. The built-in `trellis`
package has no workspace, and the name `trellis` is reserved everywhere.

Every ID a package defines starts with its full identity: participant
`ghcr.io/acme/orders-trellis.OrdersService`, API
`ghcr.io/acme/orders-trellis.orders@v1`, capability
`ghcr.io/acme/orders-trellis.orders.v1:orders.read`. The short ID is the same
without the workspace. IDL source never spells an ID. The wire, Auth, logs,
and `--format json` always carry full IDs; CLI and Console human output show the
short ID while no other installed package has the same one, and CLI input takes
a short ID when it names exactly one thing. Built-in IDs stay `trellis.auth@v1`
and `trellis.auth.v1:users.manage`.

### Authoring

An API defines models and public RPC, event, live, and operation surfaces. A
deployable participant (`service` or `device`) identifies the API it implements,
its selected dependencies, and its runtime resources. Apps and agents instead
author application request descriptors, exported through the generated `apps`
namespace; they are not installable principals. `app X { ... }` declares a
browser app (redirect sign-in); `agent X { ... }` declares a native app, such
as a desktop, mobile, or command-line tool, that signs in with Device Code
(`native app X` is not a declaration). Only the kind differs: `use`
blocks, capabilities, consent, State, and `config` are the same. The generated
request carries `kind: "browser"` or `kind: "native"`, the kind is part of the
package digest, and each sign-in entry point refuses the other kind with an
error naming both. Register the app's OAuth client with the same kind.

A use body selects whole capabilities, named `area.action`, where the action
may itself be dotted (`activation.confirmations.read`):
`required capability orders.read;` is required and `capability orders.export;`
is optional. Required wins when a capability is repeated; `use Api;` selects
nothing. `required group support;` selects an API's developer-defined group,
which stands for its current members. Generated callers expose the selected
actions; check capability availability before using an optional capability,
because selecting it does not mean it was approved. Availability has a key for
each optional capability and group, plus each member of an optional group that
allows a selected action: a member is available when the caller holds it and
its selected actions are allowed, and a group only when all of its selected
actions are, so gate each feature on the member it needs. Users approve a capability's or
group's `grants` text; changing that text makes them approve again, while
editing `title`, `description`, `allows`, or group members does not. Keep
`grants` honest, and put changes that break what users agreed to in a new API
major version. Authors declare no revision counters.
A `///` comment directly above a model, field, enum, type alias, or action
describes it. Descriptions show in the presentation IDL, `Apis.Get`, the
Console's API pages, and as Rustdoc and JSDoc on generated code, together with
each field's optionality and declared limits and each action's errors,
pagination, and capabilities; they never change a digest or compatibility.
Plain `//` comments are dropped.
Participant identity, API identity, API release version, and surface transport
version are separate concepts.

Selections must exactly match a name in the chosen API: `Get` and `Sites.Get`
are distinct. Invented prefixes are not qualifiers. Unsupported surface members
and incompatible constraints are compilation errors, not ignored options.
Numeric bounds accept finite JSON literals such as `-1` and `2.5`; string
lengths and list counts require unsigned integer literals. The IDL reference
documents each surface's members and each constraint's applicable types.
Use the `json` type for an opaque JSON value (for example free-form
configuration or details); it is carried unchecked and cannot be an event
parameter or job key. There are no string formats: a UUID or email is a
`string`, and there are no tagged unions of models.

### Dependencies

- `trellis add <path>` or `trellis add <workspace>/<name>` (such as
  `trellis add ghcr.io/acme/orders`) and `trellis rm` change dependency
  declarations. A dependency's alias is its package name; a second package of
  the same name from another workspace needs `trellis add <source> --alias
  <alias>`. `trellis rm` takes an alias, full identity, or package name, and
  refuses a package name that fits several dependencies.
- `trellis update` resolves dependencies and updates `trellis.lock`.
- `trellis install` reproduces locked dependencies and generated outputs.
- `trellis generate` compiles local IDL and generates packages using locally
  available dependencies. Use `--watch` for continuous offline generation.

Dependencies reference local or OCI native source packages: `{ package, path }`
for a local package, whose own `trellis.toml` gives its identity, or
`{ package, workspace, version }` for a published one (`trellis` alone names no
workspace). Two dependencies are the same package only when workspace and name
both match, so a package may depend on another of the same name from another
workspace under its own alias. `trellis.lock` (format 3) keys each package by
full identity and pins release and digests; each registry dependency is pulled
from the workspace it names, and a release that declares another identity is
refused. Credentials use the Docker credential configuration. `trellis publish`
pushes to the package's own `<workspace>/<name>`; the registry's access control
decides who may. If a
participant declares a durable `consumer`, add a direct `trellis` source package
dependency containing `trellis.events@v1`, choose its version in `trellis.toml`,
and run `trellis update` to lock it. Compilation fails if the dependency or the
Events API is missing; the platform does not choose a version for the contract
owner. Installation validates exact remote APIs in the global content-addressed
OCI cache, without a project-local installation tree. Direct local dependencies
contribute only requested APIs compiled from their own IDL, without recursively
resolving producer participants or manifests. Tooling supplies validated API
values to the compiler; it does not execute source-language modules. Generation
is offline; install missing remote dependencies first.

### Generated packages

Configure `[generate.rust].output` and/or `[generate.typescript].output`.
Explicit targets are authoritative and select only the named outputs; without
them, detection uses root Cargo or npm manifests, and with neither no language
package is emitted.

Each language gets one ordinary package at the source package version, with
separate `apis`, `participants`, and `apps` module namespaces rather than
independent packages or flattened root exports. TypeScript output contains
executable ESM `.js`, `.d.ts`, and `package.json`, with no consumer
transpilation step. Rust output is an ordinary path-dependency crate. Both
declare published Trellis runtime dependencies matching the CLI version.
Generation never edits the consumer's language manifests or chooses runtime
paths from repository ancestry; use normal ecosystem overrides when developing
against a local runtime.

Each package contains generated APIs, participants, types, codecs, and runtime
descriptors. Published packages contain native source and frozen resolution
metadata, not canonical API/participant JSON; native source packages are the
publication and evidence boundary. Generated descriptors are support ABI, not a
contract-as-code authoring surface.

Generated SDKs are disposable build artifacts. Commit authored IDL,
`trellis.toml`, and `trellis.lock`, not generated implementations. Run
`trellis install` before compiling local consumers, and package generated code
when distributing a consumer. Compilation, renderer, and formatter failures
preserve the last successful generated outputs. Namespace and participant
output-path collisions are errors, unrelated user files are protected, and
publication uses only short-lived staging and backups.

Generated names depend on declared action names and dependency aliases. Check
the generated participant rather than inventing a method from a generic example.
Module and export names come from short IDs (the ID without its workspace), so
they read the same whatever workspace a package is published from. Only names
that would collide change: an API whose name another API in the graph shares
is named by its short ID, then by its full ID, and names that still collide
(`ghcr.io/acme-lab/x` and `ghcr.io/acme/lab/x` both drop to `GhcrIoAcmeLabX`)
take a short hash suffix of the full ID. A participant or app that uses two
APIs of the same name gets method names from those generated names, such as
`ghcrIoAcmeLabXSamplesV1D24145caGet`; look them up in the generated package.
TypeScript participants expose flat caller methods and generated `handle...`,
`publish...`, and `on...` methods where the selection allows them. Rust
participants expose typed methods through generated facades.

### Rust models and published archives

Generated Rust ABI 2 shares primitive wire wrappers, nullable values, and cursor
pages in `trellis-protocol`. Authored model identity and wire serialization do
not change. Regenerate with the matching CLI and SDK; ABI mismatches fail
compilation. Generated Rust packages select `trellis-models` bundles directly by
exact native package identity and semantic digest, using the bundle version the
consuming Cargo graph resolves; compilation rejects a provider with a different
digest. Model bundles are versioned
independently of SDK implementation releases: old bundles can coexist with newer
SDK models, and compatible SDK fixes do not require regeneration. A model
snapshot change that alters generated Rust types takes an incompatible Cargo
version. Published model and SDK archives contain frozen sources and
need no compiler or generator build dependencies; bare Git checkouts require
preparation. Only `trellis-rs`, `trellis-protocol`, `trellis-models`, and
`trellis-testkit` are registry packages; server, compiler, and bootstrap crates
are not consumer dependencies.

## Running Trellis

### Installing the binaries

On Linux (x86_64 or arm64), `curl -fsSL https://oats-center.github.io/trellis/install.sh |
sh -s trellis` installs the CLI and `... | sh -s trellis-server` the server,
from the newest release into `~/.local/bin` after checking the release
checksum (`TRELLIS_VERSION` and `TRELLIS_INSTALL_DIR` override). Both update
themselves: `trellis upgrade` and `trellis-server upgrade`
(`--prerelease` before the first stable release), then restart the server. A
restart on a version that changed Trellis's own services installs their new
builds under the same identities. A stable release always upgrades an
installation made by an earlier stable release; only a release candidate may
refuse one made by an earlier candidate, stopping startup with the service's
name and leaving the installation unchanged. The server is also published as `ghcr.io/oats-center/trellis-server`.

### Installation and first start

An installation is a `config.toml` a person writes and the `secrets.toml`
Trellis creates beside it on its first start (every private key, owner-only).
`trellis-server config example` prints a commented `config.toml`. Plain
`trellis-server` uses `~/.config/trellis` (`/etc/trellis` with `--system`,
root's default on Linux), with data in the profile's XDG or FHS folders;
`--config <dir>` names a folder installation, which keeps everything the
server writes in `<dir>/var`. A start without `config.toml` stops and says so.

NATS belongs to an operator. Trellis takes the system account user's creds
(`[nats] system_credentials`) and an operator signing key seed
(`[nats] operator_signing_key`), signs its own `AUTH` and `TRELLIS` accounts
with the key, and sends them to the servers on every start, so the servers
need a `full` resolver. `trellis-server nats new [--servers 3] [--hosts
a,b,c] [--listen <ip>] --out <dir>` makes an operator and every server's config
for a new cluster (a cluster needs three or more servers; `--servers 1` makes
a single server) and prints the `[nats]` section. With `nsc`, `nsc edit
operator --sk generate` makes the signing key and `nsc generate creds
--account SYS` the system user. `[nats] servers` must be `tls://` unless it is
loopback or `private_network = true` (a container network only the
installation uses). `trellis-server nats <system|trellis|auth> <args>` runs the
`nats` CLI as that user; `--print` prints its creds instead.
`trellis-server admin [--config <dir>]` seeds the administrator without
starting the server or NATS.
`trellis-server backup <dir>` saves a recovery point of a running or stopped
installation while its NATS is reachable: its config, `secrets.toml` and the
files the config names, an online SQLite copy of each database,
`platform.issuer-keys/`, generated TLS, a snapshot of every JetStream stream in
Trellis's account except the lease bucket, and a checksummed `manifest.json`;
it fails, without a manifest, when the broker isn't bound to this installation
and its platform database.
`trellis-server restore <dir> [--config <dir>] [--force]` checks it and writes
it into a stopped or fresh installation, refusing one with another ID (its
`[auth] instance_id`, else `secrets.toml`'s) or an unreadable `config.toml`
unless `--force`; the next platform start loads the streams into an empty
JetStream store. An interrupted restore is run again (restore, then start),
which replaces the streams the interrupted one loaded. Leases only pick which
server runs a role: a standby needs the same NATS and, for Auth, the same database, issuer keys and `secrets.toml`.

`trellis-server --dev` runs a development installation in
`<user data>/trellis/dev` (or `--config <dir>`), creating it the first time:
plain HTTP on `localhost:3000`, or with `--host <name>` generated TLS for that
name with clients offered only the WebSocket. Only a development installation
runs its own NATS (`[nats] managed = true`): from `PATH`, otherwise it asks
before downloading the pinned, checksum-verified release; `--nats-download`
downloads without asking and `--local-nats=<path>` names an exact binary.
`--local-nats-ports=4223,8223,8081` moves its NATS client, monitor and
WebSocket ports for one run. It is never a production setup.

### TLS

`[http.transport] mode` is `tls` (supplied certificate files, reloaded when
replaced), `proxy` (an HTTPS proxy in front sends plain HTTP; `trusted_proxies`
optionally limits peers to its networks), `generated` (development and tests:
a name-constrained CA and certificate Trellis makes in its data folder and
renews within 30 days of expiry), or `loopback_development` (plain HTTP on
loopback). `generated` warns in the log, the Console and the sign-in pages.
Tests that need the production layout supply certificates from
`trellis-server tls issue --out <dir> --host <name>`, which writes
`server.crt`, `server.key` and the single-use `ca.crt` that issued them.
Clients trust a generated or other private CA only explicitly, after verifying
its SHA-256 fingerprint (`trellis-server tls status`) out of band: never
disable certificate verification and never accept a CA from broker or metadata
responses. An installation has one HTTP listener at `[http] public_origin`
(sign-in, the address the CLI, services, devices and apps connect to, and the
bundled Console at `/console`). `[console] origin` gives the Console a hostname
of its own, pointed at the same port, so its pages run apart from sign-in.
NATS TLS is the NATS operator's; `[nats] ca_certificate` names a private CA
Trellis trusts for it. Trellis reaches NATS through an HTTPS proxy with
`servers = "wss://<host>"`, checking the proxy's certificate against the
system trust store. Browser origins are trusted from registered clients'
redirect URIs, never from server configuration.

Rust participants put a private CA in `RuntimeAuthorizationTrust.root_certificates`
or pass it to `discover_native_oauth(origin, &[ca_path])`. Node participants
start with `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=<ca path>`. `trellis login <trellis-origin>`
shows an untrusted CA's fingerprint and pins it once accepted (prompt, or
`--ca-fingerprint <sha256>`); `--ca-certificate <ca path>` trusts a CA file
directly. A pinned CA that changes is a hard error. Browsers trust the CA
through the operating system or browser trust store. With
`[http] nats_websocket_upstream = "<host>:<port>"`, the Trellis port hands every
WebSocket upgrade to that NATS WebSocket listener and advertises
`wss://<trellis host>`, so one host and certificate cover both. A proxy in
front can apply the same rule itself. `[client] nats_servers = []` offers
clients only the WebSocket; the CLI, services and devices then connect over
it, so only HTTPS needs to be public. Every client presents the sentinel user
JWT the OAuth metadata publishes as `trellis.natsSentinel`, so NATS hands the
connection to Trellis's auth callout.

### OAuth portal and issuer custody

OAuth login and consent belong to Trellis's portal on the Trellis origin, never
to an app; only the bundled Console shares that origin, at `/console`, unless it
is given its own. Dex is an upstream OIDC integration-test dependency
only, never a required Trellis deployment component. Administrators brand the
portal per installation or per client from the Appearance tab of the Console's
**Sign-in** page or
`trellis theme show|set|remove [--client <id>]` (name, logo, palette, a few
headings and a footer, plus an installation-only stylesheet); changes apply at
once, and apps cannot replace the portal or change what consent shows.

Installation identity and the independently provisioned OAuth storage key
survive restarts and issuer rotation. `Issuers.Rotate` requires
`trellis.auth.v1:platform.manage`, the expected current key ID, and an
idempotency key. Auth generates and durably flushes a private successor key on
its own host, then atomically commits the old-key-signed chain link, activation,
publication intent, and replay result; replays do not rotate again, and private
keys never cross the RPC. SDKs verify the successor chain from pinned trust.
Back up the issuer seed and the Auth database's sibling
`<database-stem>.issuer-keys` directory (`platform.issuer-keys` by default) with
the database and the OAuth storage key. Restart loads the database-current key
and fails closed on missing custody.

A rotation interrupts no session: SDKs accept the old key for live use for one
authority lifetime, and every session renews onto the new key when Auth
announces the rotation. `Issuers.Revoke` is for a compromised key. It ends
that overlap at once and retires every user session holding authority the key
signed. A service or device session that already renewed onto the new key
keeps running, because it signs in with its own identity key. Revoke an old key
after the rotation has settled, not in place of rotating.

### Administrator bootstrap

Fresh startup creates the protected administrator and accepted built-in authority
before provider admission. The username defaults to `admin`. Without an initial
password, startup emits `adminAccountUrl`, a one-time password-setup link on the
Trellis origin that expires after five minutes; no default password
exists. Startup flags `--admin-username`, `--admin-password`, and
`--admin-password-stdin` configure fresh credentials. Explicit initialization
uses `trellis-server admin [--config <dir>]` with `--username` (default `admin`),
optional `--password`, or `--password-stdin`. Until password setup, each startup
prints a fresh link and invalidates prior links. After setup, restarts preserve
credentials and print no link. Explicit `--reset-admin` issues a replacement
reset link and revokes existing logins on completion; ordinary RPCs cannot reset
the protected administrator.

Fresh initialization grants only the current accepted Trellis-owned
Auth/Core/State/Health/Jobs/Events capabilities, atomically with Console/CLI
registration; the administrator holds the administrative capabilities
inherently. Replay grants no future capabilities and does not rewrite clients.
Domain API access remains explicitly granted, and Console/CLI connections still
require selection and consent: administrator status is not blanket app
authority.

### Operator CLI

The `trellis` CLI writes what a command returns (tables, records, secrets) to
stdout and its status lines (`✓` done, `•` unchanged, `!` warning), hints, and
next-step commands to stderr. Lists are aligned tables on a terminal and
headerless tab-separated rows with raw values when piped, for `cut` and `awk`.
`--format json` writes one JSON value to stdout instead and silences status
lines, and is the interface for scripts; the human layout may change between
releases. Color follows the terminal, `NO_COLOR`, `TERM=dumb` and
`CLICOLOR_FORCE`. A secret the CLI prints, such as an instance seed, root
secret, or setup code, is shown once and not kept. `svc|dev <name> remove` asks for the name unless given `-f`,
and refuses without a terminal or with `--format json` unless given `-f`.

Commands that need several values (`clients add|edit`, `apis force-replace
--source`, `roles create`, `users create|find`, `sign-in providers add`, and the
participant choice of a `--source` or `--package` command when the package has several) ask
for each required value a flag leaves out, on stderr, then show a summary and
ask to go ahead. A command given every required flag asks nothing. Without a
terminal, or with the global `--no-input`, nothing is asked: a missing required
flag fails before any write, naming every missing flag, so scripts never hang.

`trellis clients list|get|add|edit|put|disable|enable|delete` manages public OAuth
registrations, including exact loopback browser redirects. `clients add [ID]`
registers an app by asking for its kind (browser or native), title,
development flag, redirect URIs, capabilities allowed without asking, sign-up,
and optional `--source` settings declaration; each answer is also a flag
(`--kind`, `--title`, `--description`, `--[no-]development`, `--redirect-uri`,
`--allow-without-asking`, `--[no-]sign-up-password`, `--[no-]sign-up-providers`,
`--source`, `--app`). When `--source` names the app (with `--app` when the
project has several), the kind comes from its IDL declaration and a
contradicting `--kind` is refused; Auth also refuses attaching an app's
settings to a client of the other kind. `clients edit ID` asks the same questions from the
current values, or changes only the flags given. `put FILE` (`-` for stdin)
sends generated `AuthOAuthClientPutRequest` JSON for scripts. Mutations are
revision-fenced. Put keeps an existing app's enabled state, so saving a
disabled app leaves it disabled; only `clients enable` (`OAuthClients.Enable`)
turns it back on. Client flows
are fixed on every Put: browser callbacks enable Authorization Code + refresh;
native without callbacks enables Device Code + refresh; native with callbacks
enables both + refresh. Adding or removing native callbacks updates the
supported flows. Kind is immutable; use a new client ID to switch kind. Native
HTTP loopback callbacks need no development flag; browser loopback does.

Creating or applying a deployment (`trellis svc <name> create`, `svc <id>
apply`) accepts every API its participant provides that the catalog lacks or
holds at a compatible older definition, and every API it uses that the catalog
lacks, from the participant's own evidence: approving a deployment is accepting
the APIs it publishes and needs, so services can be added in any order. A
consumer never changes an accepted API; a provider that arrives later is checked
against the definition its consumer brought. A caller already running when its
provider is added renews its authority on Auth's notice and reaches it within
moments; it does not need to reconnect. `trellis apis review --source <project-root>
[--participant <package>.<Name>]` shows them first, and `apis accept` accepts
them without a deployment. An incompatible change needs `trellis apis force-replace
--source <project-root> [--participant <package>.<Name>]`, which shows each
changed API's review and asks for, or takes, `--acknowledge-breakage` and
`--acknowledge-consent-impact`; it needs `trellis.auth.v1:apis.forceReplace`.
`apis force-replace FILE` sends generated `AuthApiForceReplaceRequest` JSON
instead, for role or mapping edits. Console exposes OAuth clients and the
API catalog.

The Console's Add service form takes only the service's `trellis.toml` and
`.trellis` files (or their folder), no `trellis.lock`. `Auth.Packages.Resolve`
(`trellis.auth.v1:users.manage`, like `Deployments.Create`) builds the package
evidence from them: each dependency comes from packages supplied with the
request, the `trellis` package the server ships, or an installed participant's
packages, by full identity and version requirement (a path dependency takes
any version and means the supplied package of its name, else the `localhost`
or built-in one; the highest match wins and the result says which). A dependency none
of these satisfy is returned by name and requirement for the caller to supply;
nothing is fetched from a registry. The returned evidence goes to
`Deployments.Create`, which checks it like any other.

A service published with `trellis publish` is installed from its release
instead, so its container connects at once with nothing to approve:
`trellis svc <name> create --package <workspace>/<name>@<version>
[--participant <package>.<Name>]`, and for a new release `trellis svc <id>
apply --package <workspace>/<name>@<version>` before rolling out its image
(`dev create|apply` take the same flags). `<workspace>/<name>@sha256:<manifest
digest>`, as `publish` prints, pins exactly the reviewed release. `--package`
and `--source` exclude each other. `Auth.Packages.Pull` (`users.manage`) does
the work for the CLI and the Console's "From a published package" option alike:
it pulls the release from the package's own workspace and accepts it only when
it declares that identity, checks the manifest, config, and source digests,
pulls each dependency from its own workspace by the digest its frozen
resolution records, compiles from exactly those packages and the built-in
`trellis` package without resolving again, and returns the evidence and
participants for `Create` or `Apply`. A release whose bytes don't match its
digests is refused. Registry credentials are Auth state, not server config:
`trellis registries set <name> --prefix <workspace> [--username <user>
--secret-file <path|->]`, `registries list|remove`, or the Console's Services >
Package registries (`Auth.PackageRegistries.*`); Docker Hub's prefix is
`docker.io/<org>`. Trellis signs in to a
workspace with the registry added for it and pulls anonymously when there is
none; a private registry's secret is sealed with the storage key and never
returned.

A running service updates itself. When its generated participant digest differs
from the revision its instance runs, the service SDK submits its package evidence
(`Auth.ServiceUpdates.Submit`, which every service instance may call) and
connects again once Auth installs it. A build that asks for no capability,
resource, or API the deployment does not already hold installs at once,
accepting compatible new revisions of the APIs it already provides. A build that
asks for more, including reattaching a resource an earlier build dropped or
starting to provide an API, waits for an administrator: the SDK logs the Console review link
(`/console/admin/services/<deploymentId>?update=<updateId>`) and prints it as a
terminal QR code (an installation without the Console has no link, so it prints
`trellis svc <deployment-id> approve`), and `trellis svc <deployment-id> updates|approve|reject` does
the same from the CLI. Dropping a resource only detaches it; its data stays until
`Resources.Remove`, and an approved reattachment brings it back. A build that
implements an API another deployment already serves needs an explicit
acknowledgement on approval (`acknowledgeSharedApis`, or
`approve --acknowledge-shared-apis`), and so do `Deployments.Create`/`Apply`
(`svc create|apply --acknowledge-shared-apis`): both deployments then share the API's queue
group, so requests split at random between services with separate data. Scale or
move a service with more instances of one deployment instead. A build whose
implemented API changed incompatibly is refused until the API is force-replaced.
`trellis svc <deployment-id> apply --package|--source` installs a build ahead of time instead, which is the approval.

A service whose IDL the administrator does not have, such as a third party's,
starts from a claim: `trellis svc <name> create --public-key <key>` without
`--package` or `--source` (or `Auth.ServiceClaims.Create` with its public key)
creates one; without `--public-key` the CLI generates the identity and prints
its seed once. The first service to connect with that identity submits itself
as the claim's update. Approving it (`trellis svc <claim-id> approve`, or the Console review
link) creates the deployment, accepts the APIs it provides and the unaccepted
ones it uses, and provisions an
instance holding that identity; the service then connects as that instance.

For `trellis identity grants set`, the input file contains only
`installedRevision`, `grants`, and `expiresAt`; all three are required.
`installedRevision` accepts a JSON integer or decimal string in
`1..=9007199254740991`; `expiresAt` accepts `null`, or a JSON integer or decimal
string in `0..=9007199254740991`. Omitting `--expected-revision` uses the current
binding revision, or zero for creation; a stale revision is rejected without
changing the binding.

### Local state

Keep the platform database and NATS JetStream data together. Before it writes
anything to a broker, every Trellis role checks the broker's identity record:
a broker of another installation, or one bound to a different platform
database, refuses startup and is left untouched. Restore the matching store, or
use fresh platform and JetStream state and provision deployments again. A role
started apart from the platform waits until its platform has bound a new
broker. Recreating consumers and buckets alone does not recover job
keys or stored objects. Rust and Node replicas use one deployment-scoped
Operation storage codec; this pre-release cutover does not migrate earlier
records, so retain existing installations unchanged and use fresh
development/test state. Unsupported records fail visibly; the runtime never
deletes or recreates them as empty state.

Runtime data has explicit retention. `[events] history_retention_days`
(default 90) keeps the recorded event history beyond the event stream's 7 days;
`[events] dead_letter_retention_days` (default 90, at least 7) keeps resolved
and dismissed dead letters, while open ones stay until settled;
`[jobs] history_retention_days` (default 30) bounds the job lifecycle streams
and settled jobs, while failed and dead jobs stay for retry and replay; a job
no worker claims within it expires with an error saying so. A
changed limit is applied to the existing streams at the next start.
`Health.Storage`, the Console Health page, and the `trellis.storage.bytes`,
`trellis.storage.records` and `trellis.storage.oldest.age` gauges report each
data class's size and oldest record.

For several development installations on one machine, give each its own
`--dev --config <dir>` folder, then its own `[http] port` and `nats.conf`
ports. The development defaults are 3000/4222/8222/8080; installations use a
30-second owner lease renewed every 5 seconds.

### Health

Provisioned services and devices publish the native `Health.Heartbeat` event
automatically, using ordinary SessionEvent signatures and the runtime-only
`trellis.health.v1:health.report` capability that Auth assigns through native
provisioning; users and apps cannot obtain it. The collector verifies whole
catalog authority, broker chronology, retirement cutoff, and signed
deployment/instance identity; the signed `trellis.nativeParticipant.v1`
extension supplies installed revision and participant digest, never payload
claims. No health declaration is needed in service contracts, and initial
publication does not gate connection.

A participant can add its own version, structured details, and named checks to
every heartbeat; checks run at each publication. A check reports `ok`,
`degraded` or `failed`. Any failed check makes the instance unhealthy;
otherwise any degraded check makes it degraded; otherwise it is healthy.
Checks an SDK adds itself count like any other, so the rule reads the same in
every language.

Each service heartbeat also carries its lifecycle `phase`: `connecting`,
`serving` or `stopping`, published again at once on every change.

### Readiness, stop and upgrades

A service serves once it is connected, its build is installed (approved if it
asked for new access), its required settings are set, and every handler, job
worker and consumer registered before the SDK's serve call (`wait()`, `run()`)
takes work. None of them takes a job or delivery before that call. With
`NOTIFY_SOCKET` set, both SDKs send systemd `READY=1` once serving,
`STOPPING=1` when stopping, and `STATUS=` text (connecting, waiting for
approval with the review link, waiting for settings with their names, serving,
reconnecting, stopping), so `Type=notify` and Quadlet `Notify=true`
need no health check. An optional readiness probe in the runtime options, a
file present only while serving and/or HTTP `GET /ready` (200 serving, else
503) and `GET /live` (200 until stopped), serves orchestrators such as
Kubernetes. Serving goes false while the connection is lost and reconnecting;
a build no longer installed for its instance stops with an error.

SIGTERM, SIGINT, or the SDK's stop call stops a service gracefully: it leaves
every queue group, ends its Live streams with `local_shutdown`, waits up to the
stop timeout (25 s by default) for requests, event deliveries and jobs it
holds, then hands what still runs back with no delay (jobs are cancelled for
shutdown, deliveries are naked; a job handler that ignores its cancellation is
not waited for, even after its lease was lost, and its result is discarded) and
exits. A job or delivery it receives after the stop began goes straight back
without running. Operations still recover through lease expiry. Do not install
signal handlers in service code.

Upgrade by overlapping: run each process as its own instance, start the new
build, wait until it serves, stop the old one. `trellis svc <ID> instances`
(`--format json`) and the Console service page show each instance's build,
whether it is current or older, its state, its health with the name and
message of each failing check, connected-at and last heartbeat. A connected
instance whose heartbeats stopped shows `offline` health beside the state it
last reported. A
build that drops an API or a resource such as a job queue the older build
declares, or that replaces an API with its next major, stops older builds at
once; add the new major beside the old one and drop the old one in a later
build. See /guides/upgrade-without-downtime.

## Identity And Connection

### Participants and admission

Services and devices are deployable principals that present a signed
provisioned admission in NATS CONNECT; there is no HTTP bootstrap. Browser and
native apps obtain a DPoP-bound OAuth token whose signed Trellis admission
authorizes CONNECT for a fresh runtime key. These are different identity
lifecycles, not interchangeable shortcuts. Neither accepts a raw NATS URL/JWT or
a client-authored assignment as authority.

Provisioned services and devices prove possession of their identity key and a
fresh runtime/session key for the configured installation/account. Auth derives
their deployment, instance, participant, and implementation authority from
current provisioning records; clients never assert those bindings during
CONNECT. Provisioning supplies broker endpoints and pinned installation/issuer
trust; obtain trust from initialization or authenticated provisioning, never an
unsigned discovery response. Immediate `ServiceInstances.Provision` and
`Devices.Provision` require `identityPublicKey` from a client-owned Ed25519 key;
Trellis never stores or returns its private seed. From the CLI, whoever runs
the service makes the key with `trellis keys new`, keeps the seed, and gives
the administrator the public key for
`trellis svc <id> provision --public-key <key>`, which registers it or selects
the instance that already has it. A bare `provision` generates the key pair
itself and prints the seed once. Missing `identityPublicKey` returns
`identity_public_key_required` without provisioning or consuming the
idempotency key, and `provisioningSecret` is null. `ServiceInstances.Provision`
awaits the native resource producer before success (empty declarations and KV
are supported; other declarations fail explicitly). Retry the same request after
broker failure; retained allocations are never destroyed.

### Enrolled service instances

For processes that come and go (Kubernetes pods, rolling releases), issue the
deployment an enrollment secret instead of provisioning each instance:
`trellis svc <id> enrollment issue` prints it once (Trellis keeps only its
hash). A process given it, through the SDK option or
`TRELLIS_ENROLLMENT_SECRET`, makes its own identity key, registers it with a
signed `POST /auth/service/enroll`, and connects with that key through ordinary
admission; the secret never reaches NATS. A seed and a secret together are an
error. Each secret has an instance cap (20), an hourly rate (100), an optional
expiry, and `currentBuildOnly` (its instances' own `ServiceUpdates.Submit` is
refused, so install builds with `svc <id> apply` first). At the cap a new
enrollment replaces the secret's longest-offline instance, never a connected
one or one enrolled within the first-connect grace (10 min) that has not
connected yet; otherwise it is refused (`instance_limit`). Retrying an
enrollment with the same key returns the same instance, even at the cap or
rate. A memory-only key enrolls a new instance per start and retires it at a
graceful stop (`ServiceInstances.RetireOwn`); with a key file the process keeps
its instance: it connects with the stored key first, stops when an
administrator removed the instance, and enrolls a new key only when Auth
reports the old one retired or unregistered (`POST /auth/service/identity`). An
enrolled instance retired while it was disconnected stops, and its restart
enrolls anew. Enrolled instances offline past the retirement period (24 h,
`Auth.InstancePolicy`, per deployment or installation) are retired; disabled
deployments are skipped, and provisioned instances only with
`retireProvisioned`. `enrollment revoke --retire-instances` revokes a leaked
secret and disconnects everything it created. Instance states are `active`,
`disabled`, `removed`, and `retired` (with `retiredReason`); `origin` says
`provisioned` or `enrolled`.

Auth Callout resolves the deployment, installed artifacts, capabilities,
resources, online issuer, inbox, and exact transport permissions, and returns
signed session authority that clients verify. Own-context bootstrap signs the
exact physical socket's broker `attachmentId` and verifies its echoed signed
registry ID; overlapping sockets never select the newest attachment as a
fallback.

### Devices and companions

Provisioning a device without `identityPublicKey` issues a one-use
provisioning secret bound to the server-owned instance; `/auth/device/enroll`
verifies durable and ephemeral key possession. `Devices.Reviews.Get/Decide`
require the device's confirmation code and expected revision. Completed
activation rechecks authenticate the retained challenge instead of opening
another review; local completion never authorizes a disabled or removed device.

A device companion is a native OAuth application request with independent user
consent, credential custody, and connection. Accepted deployment registration
creates the dedicated client `trellis.device.<deploymentId>.companion` but grants
no user authority. Declare Auth's `deviceCompanionsManage` capability in the
companion request, complete ordinary explicit Device Code consent, and invoke
`DeviceCompanions.Attach` from that authenticated grant; parent credentials
cannot substitute. A required wrapper refuses a missing companion; an optional
wrapper can connect without it. `DeviceCompanions.Revoke` removes the
association and revokes only its exact grant and refresh families, leaving other
grants, the user login, and parent authority independent. The associated user
or an administrator with current delegated `trellis.auth.v1:users.manage` may
remove it. Removing the declaration rejects new and pending consent, while
existing independently consented grants retain ordinary refresh. Parent and
child maintain separate connections and revocation.

### Browser and native sign-in

Browser sign-in uses OAuth Authorization Code with PKCE and DPoP. Public,
credential-free discovery and issuer-chain metadata are readable before an
unknown application's HTTPS CIMD document is prepared; client-bound token CORS
and cookie-authenticated Portal routes remain separate. Auth validates client
metadata retrieval, exact redirects, consent, and proof bindings. Sign-in
carries a reusable signed intent; a bounded authentication transaction starts
only when authentication begins, not when the portal renders, and only one
outstanding attempt can claim an intent. Persist the pending portal binding
before the start request and reuse it after response loss or reload:
same-binding retries recover the active transaction, another binding conflicts.
Detached progress requires the initiating key's fresh proof, and portal
rendering exposes no transaction discovery. Denied, expired, or consumed
attempts can restart from the same intent.

The SDK validates OAuth state, callback, PKCE, and DPoP bindings before
retaining credentials. Browser custody uses nonextractable keys in IndexedDB and
cross-tab refresh ownership; Rust native custody uses owner-only files and a
cross-process family lock; Node custody is process-local memory unless the
application supplies a provider. Device Code needs a native OAuth client: against
a browser client, `/device_authorization` answers `unauthorized_client` with an
`error_description` naming both kinds. A valid login can authenticate new consent
without another password. Invalid login requires authentication; valid-login
authorization denial surfaces its machine code and is not a reason to start a
login loop. Consent cannot grant missing account entitlement.

### Refresh and renewal

OAuth sessions retain their original verified refresh family. CONNECT,
`Authority.Renew`, `OwnContextGet`, and `Admission.Renew` consult that exact
family's revocation and absolute deadline; a different live family of the same
grant cannot replace it, and rotation never extends it. `Admission.Renew` uses
the live caller's session-key proof and own context digest to return same-key
signed admission, at most 300 seconds and bounded by the candidate
authority/family, without rotating refresh tokens. Invalid roots retire the
session and enqueue cutoff/kicks. Provisioned admission still needs the
client's identity signature (`provisioned_signature_required`).

Cold OAuth resume verifies signed issuer successors from the retained pin using
`GET /.well-known/trellis/issuer-chain` at the selected Trellis origin and
persists successor trust before spending a refresh token. Unavailable or invalid
chains leave it unspent. A returned new token survives later issuer
verification failure, but its admission stays unusable until authenticated.
Never retry an ambiguously spent predecessor; a lost refresh response requires
recovery, not token replay. Discovery cannot replace a retained issuer pin; only
an authenticated rotation chain advances it. Already-open browser tabs refresh
discovery from retained trust before spending refresh tokens. Rejected
cross-user Device Code reauthorization preserves existing credentials.

Transport recovery reuses admission only while shared verification accepts its
lifetime and current pinned trust; transport loss alone does not spend refresh
custody. Renewal checks the selected HTTP origin before spending the token, and
an ambiguous token POST still requires explicit recovery. Native renewal uses
the current maintenance attachment through verified authority promotion,
including after transport replacement. If no safe native carrier survives,
fresh admission may replace a missed retired logical session under the same
valid provisioned credential and pinned trust; removed permissions are not
restored, and revoked roots or shutdown cannot recover. Preparation retries
never retransmit application requests or clear known revocations. Auth sends
no unsigned refusal, so a renewal it doesn't answer, as when it is overloaded,
runs again a second later and the connection stays open; only a signed answer
that retires or reduces the session ends it. Expired authority still can't
authorize application work while renewal keeps trying.

### Authority on a live connection

The libraries own proofs, context verification, proactive refresh, and transport
maintenance. Session authority, admission credentials, transport endpoints,
grants, clock offset, and issuer keys are process-memory-only. Renewing
unchanged transport authority promotes the new session authority without
replacing a healthy socket. Newly approved authority is adopted automatically on
a readied successor, while safe accepted work retains its receiving connection.
Retain the logical client, generated facades, and still-bound resources across
these changes; no manual transport refresh or upgrade notification exists. Old
sockets close after their retained work releases them. Reduced or revoked
authority, physical failure, and hard authorization deadlines can interrupt
affected work. Raw NATS connections are physical attachments, not
generation-aware application handles. A lost connection is never reconnected
in place: the SDK opens a fresh connection admitted with current authority,
recreates subscriptions on it, and then routes requests. A request made during
the gap, or one whose connection is lost while it is being signed, waits for
it within its deadline and is never sent after the deadline.

Live authority requires a verified initial revocation snapshot and continuing
coverage; epoch fencing prevents old watchers from changing successor coverage.
Fresh application IO cannot proceed while own revocation coverage is
unavailable: bounded acquisitions wait within their budget, immediate ones report
unavailability. Mirror rollover stages the replacement without withdrawing
healthy predecessor coverage, and replacement IO stays fenced until authenticated
replay and checked handover. On mirror failure, one cancellable private
supervisor restores coverage on the surviving attachment while application IO
remains fenced; it neither clears known revocations nor retransmits application
requests. If authority expires during coverage loss, private admission obtains
and verifies fresh authority before application use resumes; snapshot recovery
alone never extends expired authority. Jobs and durable event intake keep
bounded capacity across generations, with each delivery retaining its receiving
connection through disposition.

Native providers finish accepted RPCs across ordinary authority promotion by
reacquiring a coherent current signing snapshot within one configured deadline.
Handlers are not redispatched, and provider, issuer, expiry, and revocation
checks remain mandatory. Accepted finite responses may outlive the opening
caller context, but not their request deadline; expired evidence cannot start
new work.

Already admitted connections resolve public verification metadata through the
read-only `trellis.auth.metadata.get` bootstrap; there is no typed Auth RPC for
it and no admin capability is needed. Its issuer-signed responses resolve only
requested authority material, logical status/cutoff, or pinned issuer rotation
chains. Clients verify signatures, retained nonce/subject/reply/scope, and
freshness against pinned trust; missing or unavailable responses never clear
revocation or grant authority. Historical issuer keys are resolved the same way,
authenticated by the active pinned issuer or its forward-verified successor.
They never advance live trust; compromised keys remain unusable. A retired
catalog signer does not invalidate an immutable catalog referenced by current
signed authority.

### Logout

Trellis HTTP endpoints serve bootstrap, browser/account flows, recovery, and
browser assets; connected Trellis control uses generated APIs over NATS. Use the
connected client's `logout()` for normal sign-out so local installation and
connection state are updated together. Auth holds the caller's own revocation
and disconnect for five seconds so the `Sessions.Logout` reply arrives first;
Auth refuses the session from the cutoff. If a reply is still lost, `logout()`
confirms revocation through signed HTTP recovery. Unrelated authorization
failures do not count as successful logout.

Ending the Portal login (the `end_session_endpoint`, `/logout`) does not end
the OIDC provider's session. Every app sign-out through `/logout` marks the
browser, even when no Portal login was left to end; a Portal login that expires
does not. The browser's next OIDC sign-in sends the provider's
`promptAfterSignOut` setting (Auth DB, `Auth.OIDCProviders.Put`, Console
provider form, `trellis sign-in providers add|edit --prompt-after-sign-out`):
`login` (default, `prompt=login`, asks for credentials if the provider supports
it), `selectAccount` (`prompt=select_account`, an account chooser, not proof of
a fresh sign-in), `consent` (`prompt=consent`, re-approval, not proof of a
fresh sign-in), or `none` (no prompt; the provider may sign the person straight
back in). Later sign-ins reuse the provider's session again. If the provider
refuses the prompt (`login_required`, `interaction_required`,
`consent_required`, `account_selection_required`, or `invalid_request` about
`prompt`), the sign-in page names the setting and the browser's next try with
that provider goes without the prompt; other providers still get theirs.

## Authorization

### Model

Auth owns API-scoped capability grants, roles, OAuth consent, deployment
implementation rights, and resource allocations; installing IDL grants nothing
by itself. Auth unions valid entitlements and intersects them with the declared
selection and approved consent in one authoritative transaction. Signed logical
session authority is immutable; a reduction retires every live digest under that
session ID. Compatible catalog expansion requires renewal and cannot silently
approve declined capabilities. Signed revocations remain effective through
mirror reconnect or missing entries until context acceptance deadlines expire.
Service and device authority is deployment-owned and separate from
independently consented user companion authority. Read-only capabilities do not
grant write access.

Capability approvals are policy decisions over whole capabilities, not saved
exact-action grant snapshots. Holding a group grants its current members, so a
membership change reaches holders at once; an app keeps the members its user
consented to until the user approves again. Capability discovery does not grant
authority. Own-authority and session maintenance are fixed session rights, not
ordinary capability requests.

`Auth.Capabilities.List` accepts optional `participantId`, `revision`, and
`sourceApi` filters. A participant plus revision selects an exact retained
snapshot; omitting revision selects that participant's current installation, and
revision requires a participant. With neither scope filter, discovery uses every
participant's current installation. Entries include `sourceApi` and `apiDigest`:
identical API definitions deduplicate, while differing definitions under the
same API ID remain distinct. Do not select an arbitrary definition by capability
identity alone.

### Consent

Existing grants are reused only when shared issuance/policy semantics prove
compatibility without expanding approved authority; neither activity nor a
matching revision alone establishes eligibility. Compatible revision changes do
not force consent. Additional authority eligible for approval presents fresh
consent after authentication without a second password prompt. Stale consent
decisions are rejected and refreshed; policy denial is an authorization error,
while unavailable runtime/resource evidence remains bounded pending.

Explicit one-off consent overrides older remembered choices without changing
them. Reused choices retain their expiry; later shared withdrawals still retire
affected sessions. A shortened effective authorization deadline is a reduction
unless another entitlement path preserves the outstanding authority. Deadlines
on newly gained rights bound new contexts, not older narrower contexts or the
logical-session root. Consent approval binds the current server-owned
presentation and the selected optional capabilities; stale forms require a fresh
presentation. Signed session authority has a shared 64 KiB issuer,
verification, and parsing budget.

Configured implied consent applies only to registered browser bindings and their
bounded capability subset; a listed group allows its current members. Saving a
client that allows an administrative capability without asking requires
`trellis.auth.v1:platform.manage`. Native and Device Code clients require explicit user
approval even when registered, and Device Code confirmation remains mandatory.

Provisional CIMD client intake shares a 128-client/16 MiB budget and a
five-minute lifetime; live decisions and approved refresh lifecycles are
retained. Exhaustion returns `temporarily_unavailable`, not administrative
registration or authority.

OIDC claim refresh is scoped to the selected provider and upstream subject; a
second linked identity cannot add or remove another identity's mapped roles.
Direct grants remain independent of upstream role loss and claim freshness.

Mark a role "give to new users" (`assignToNewUsers` on `Auth.Roles.Put`, the
Console role form, or `trellis roles create|edit --new-users`) to give every
user created afterwards a base set of permissions. Each gets an ordinary role
assignment an administrator can revoke; existing users are unchanged.

Sign-in methods are Auth state changed live, never configuration: the Methods
tab of the Console's Sign-in page, `trellis sign-in set`, or
`Auth.SignInSettings.Update` turn username-and-password sign-in and local self
sign-up on or off and set the minimum password length (`passwordMinLength`,
`--password-min-length`, 8 to 128 characters, 8 by default) for new and changed
passwords. The minimum counts Unicode code points, not bytes. OIDC sign-in
has no switch: it is on while at least one provider is enabled. Auth refuses a change that would leave local users off and no provider
enabled. Providers are managed on that page or with
`trellis sign-in providers list|show|add|edit|enable|disable|remove`; `add` prints the
provider's ID, which `Auth.Users.Find` takes, and the callback URL
(`<Trellis origin>/portal/oidc/callback`) to register with the provider, and
reads the client secret from `--client-secret-file` (`-` for standard input).
Auth trusts a provider's certificate through the system trust store. For a
provider on a private CA, confirm the SHA-256 fingerprint of the issuer that
ends its chain with the provider's operator and pin it: the Console's
Certificate fingerprint field, `--certificate-fingerprint <sha256>`, or
`certificateFingerprint` on `Auth.OIDCProviders.Put` (`null` removes it,
`edit --no-certificate-fingerprint` in the CLI). Auth checks the fingerprint
against the chain the provider presents and trusts that issuer for that
provider only. Adding a provider nothing vouches for is refused with the
fingerprint it presents. Removing a pin is saved even while the provider still
needs it; its sign-ins then fail until it is pinned again. Custom
authorization parameters (`authorizationParameters` on `Auth.OIDCProviders.Put`,
the Console provider form, `--authorization-param NAME=VALUE`, repeatable;
`edit` replaces the list when any are given, `--clear-authorization-params`
empties it) are added to every sign-in and linking request to the provider,
such as `organization=<org id>` for an Auth0 application that requires an
organization. At most 16, unique names of letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.`;
names Auth sets itself (`client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `response_type`, `scope`,
`state`, `nonce`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method`, `prompt`) are
refused, and so is `response_mode`, because the callback reads only the query. Auth does not check the ID token against them (an Auth0 `org_id` is
not verified). `disable` and
`enable` (`Auth.OIDCProviders.Disable/Enable`) turn a provider off and back on.
People can create their
own account only where the installation allows it and the app they are signing
in to does too (`trellis clients sign-up <app> --password|--providers`, the
Console app form, or `Auth.OAuthClients.SignUp.Update`). New accounts get the
roles marked for new users.

### Administrative capabilities

Administrative Auth RPCs are allowed by the administrative capability that names
them: `trellis.auth.v1:accounts.manage`, `trellis.auth.v1:users.manage`,
`trellis.auth.v1:roles.manage`,
`trellis.auth.v1:apis.accept`, `trellis.auth.v1:apis.forceReplace`,
`trellis.auth.v1:clients.manage`, and `trellis.auth.v1:platform.manage`. They
are ordinary capabilities in a namespace only built-in Trellis contracts may
use. Roles, direct grants, and identity-provider mappings can carry them;
changing who holds one requires `trellis.auth.v1:platform.manage`. Auth rechecks
current entitlements on every call.

Services request them the same way, in the service's IDL:

```trellis
service AccountJanitor {
  use auth { required capability accounts.manage; }
}
```

The service then calls `Users.Find` and `Users.Delete` through the methods its
`TrellisService` exposes. Deploying a service that selects an administrative
capability requires `trellis.auth.v1:platform.manage`, which the initialized
administrator holds; approval grants the capability to the deployment. An
operator with it deploys the service with
`trellis svc <name> create --source <package> --participant AccountJanitor`, or
creates a claim with `trellis svc <name> create` and, once the service has
connected and submitted itself, approves it with `trellis svc <claim-id> approve`.
A running service whose new build adds an administrative capability waits for
`trellis svc <deployment-id> approve` the same way.

Apps request administrative capabilities like any other, through their generated
required/optional selections; there is no separate privilege request. Optional
administration is never preselected or remembered. Delegating one to an app has
two safeguards, on by default under `[auth.administration]`: a separate consent
confirmation and registered clients only. The initialized administrator holds
all seven inherently, and everything else through an editable Administrator role. Localhost or
development mode establishes no trust, and the Console and every application
stay on origins of their own, apart from the Trellis origin.

### Verification

Message proofs bind the authority digest, exact API/action identity, API
generation/revision, actual subject, message identity, and exact payload bytes.
The signed authority supplies the originating session public key; message
headers do not establish another identity or carry permission lists.

Request verification checks caller grants against the caller's exact signed
catalog reference, independently of the provider's pinned implementation and
certificate. Compatible accepted revisions within one API generation need not
match; neither catalog grants additional rights to the other party.

Provider-owned event publication requires the exact issuer-verified
event-publish action in the certificate bound to the signed native authority,
deployment, instance, implementation, API generation, and action introduction
revision. It does not require consumer capabilities. Delegated publication uses
whole-capability membership. Provider certificates never grant RPC caller or
event-consumption rights.

Historical event verification requires both the signed event timestamp and
trusted original JetStream publication metadata (`published` and
`stream_sequence`). Both timestamps must fall within the publisher authority's
validity window and precede any ordinary session revocation cutoff; certified
publication also requires both within the provider certificate's validity
window. A consumer's read time is not publication evidence, so a backdated
signature cannot authenticate a new publication after expiry or revocation.
Current permission to read is a separate check from past publisher
authenticity. Ordinary certificate expiry or issuer retirement does not
invalidate authentic retained publications, including cold replay; compromised
issuers remain unusable. Applications do not implement their own verifier or
inspect Trellis's internal authorization registry.

## Accounts And Directory

Every active user holds the `trellis.auth.v1:account` group without a role or
grant: their own profile, password, sign-ins, linked sign-ins, connected apps,
device links, and app settings. No role or grant can take it away. An app
still gets these capabilities only when the user consents, and each of their
RPCs acts on the caller's own account.

- `accountRead` reveals your own profile (names, email and verification status,
  and photo), account details, and current session, and permits signing out of
  the current login and its application sessions. `Users.Resolve` is self-only
  and includes the caller's `account`; `Sessions.Me` and `Sessions.Logout`
  require normal selection and consent. None of this grants directory access.
  `accountRead` also permits `Runtime.Version`, the server's version; a caller
  with an administrative capability also gets any newer release as `update`.
- `usersRead`, selected and consented, permits `Users.List/Get`: an active-user
  directory with immutable `principalId`, names, available email, and photos.
  Ordinary results omit `account`. Delegated and currently held
  `trellis.auth.v1:accounts.manage` additionally exposes username, password status,
  and lifecycle/revision, and permits inactive-user lookup and username search.
- `accountProfileWrite` permits `Users.Profile.Update` on your own names, manual
  unverified email, and picture source (`pictureProviderId` of a linked OIDC
  sign-in, or `useGravatar`). Use the self
  account's `profileRevision` and an idempotency key. Omitted fields stay
  unchanged; clear flags restore eligible linked-provider values. Manual choices
  survive OIDC login, and matching-sub bounded UserInfo enriches presentation
  only. Email equality never links identities.
- `accounts.manage` permits `Users.Find/Create/Update/Delete` and
  `Users.PasswordReset.Create` on every account but the default
  administrator's, whatever the account holds. `Users.Find` takes exactly one
  key, `userId` or `identity: { providerId, subject }` (the configured
  provider's Trellis ID and the upstream `sub`, matched exactly; never email
  or username), finds disabled accounts too, and returns `found` with the
  `user` (lifecycle and revision in `user.account.principal`) and its linked
  `identities`; a miss is an absent `found`, not an error. Check that the
  identity is still listed before acting on the user. A
  `Users.Delete` retry after a lost reply gets `AuthError` `not_found`; treat
  that as done. `Users.Update` checks lifecycle `expectedRevision`; omitted
  profile fields are untouched, and intentional profile changes also require
  `expectedProfileRevision`. A stale combined save rolls back both.
  `Users.Delete` signs the account out everywhere and removes its sign-ins,
  profile, and access; its username becomes free.
- `accounts.manage` also permits `Users.Identities.Link` and
  `Users.Identities.Unlink` with `{ userId, identity: { providerId, subject },
  expectedRevision, idempotencyKey }` (`expectedRevision` is
  `user.account.principal.revision`); both return `{ user, identities }`.
  It permits `Users.IdentityLink.Providers` too, to choose the provider.
  Linking needs an enabled provider and an enabled account; the person's next
  sign-in through that provider with that exact `sub` opens the account, even
  with sign-up off, and refreshes its OIDC profile fields and mapped roles.
  Until then the identity adds no profile field and nothing verified. Linking
  a sign-in the account already has is a no-op success; one another account
  has fails with `AuthError` code `identity_linked_to_another_user`.
  `Users.Create` takes optional `identities` (same shape) linked atomically
  with the creation. Unlink ends the sign-ins made with it and is refused
  when it would leave the account no way to sign in. CLI:
  `trellis users create ... --provider <id> --subject <sub>`,
  `trellis users link|unlink <user> --provider <id> --subject <sub>`. To
  migrate users keyed by ID from another system, create each with its
  provider `sub` in `identities` and re-key to the returned `principalId`.

A handler sees its own caller's profile without any directory capability: a
verified user caller carries `user` with `displayName`, optional `givenName`,
`familyName`, `email` and `avatarUrl`, and `emailVerified`, as Auth signed them into the
session's authority (later profile edits appear once Auth reissues it). Service
and device callers carry no `user`. Use `usersRead` only to look up other users.

Names and email are not unique identity keys. Key application-owned
authorization by immutable `principalId`; a directory match does not grant
access to application records.

`avatarUrl` (directory results and `caller.user`) is a stable Trellis-hosted
image URL for the current profile revision, like an OIDC `picture`. A new photo
or profile change gets a new URL, and a disabled account's URL stops serving.
Render with `referrerpolicy="no-referrer"` and show local initials on error; a
current URL for someone with no picture answers `204 No Content`, which an
`<img>` also treats as an error.
Revoking `usersRead` stops new URLs, not already issued ones. Without a chosen
OIDC sign-in picture, any email, verified or not, falls back to Gravatar,
which receives its normalized SHA-256 hash; the hash remains personal
information. Operators disable all
remote-derived images, including cached ones, with
`auth.avatar.external_fetch_enabled=false`.

`Users.PasswordReset.Create` targets `userId` and returns a five-minute, one-use
token for `/account/reset?token=...` on the Trellis origin. Completion checks
Origin/CSRF, credential CAS, and the requester's original active logical session
and current `trellis.auth.v1:accounts.manage` with the target still in reach,
then atomically changes the password
and revokes login/grant families. Bootstrap administrators use local recovery
instead.

`UserIdentities.List`, `UserIdentities.Unlink`, and `Users.IdentityLink.Create`
target the current user. `Users.IdentityLink.Providers` lists the providers, by
ID and name, that link creation accepts. Linking returns a five-minute portal URL and requires
the exact initiating user and fresh verified upstream OIDC with nonce/PKCE;
provider changes and identities owned by another user are rejected. Creation
replay keeps the original sealed response and never revives an action.
Last-sign-in-method and protected-administrator checks remain. Approval is a
protected same-origin POST whose no-store continuation page links to a
60-second, one-use GET handoff bound to the portal session, provider, and
account; top-level navigation reaches the verified IdP without relaxing
`form-action 'self'` or leaking the handoff in referrers. Direct, expired, and
replayed handoffs fail.

`Auth.Connections.List` accepts `principalId` to filter physical connections.

## Communication Surfaces

- RPC: a typed request and response, including declared business errors.
- Event: a published fact. Durable consumption uses participant-declared
  Consumer resources and can redeliver; handlers need a duplicate-handling
  strategy for their side effects.
- Live: connection-scoped live data. Closing or aborting the subscription
  cancels provider work; it is not durable event history.
- Operation: caller-visible asynchronous work with progress, terminal output,
  and optional cancellation, updates, or transfer.
- Job: service-private queued execution with retries and lifecycle state.

### Routing

RPC, Operation starts, and Live openings use canonical generated API/action
subjects. Providers sharing a logical API share request queues and must be
suitable alternatives; identical IDL does not make independent databases or
physical devices interchangeable. Signed provider identity, generation/action
checks, and service-owned resources remain separate from caller capabilities.
Established Live/Transfer traffic and existing Operation controls retain
owner-directed routing. There is no persisted caller-to-deployment selection or
automatic retry of potentially executed requests. This decision is still being
integrated on this branch.

### RPC

RPC cancellation stops the caller's wait, not work already accepted by the
service; neither cancellation nor an elapsed deadline undoes accepted work. Use
Operation cancellation for business work. A no-responders reply means no
provider received the request, so the SDKs send the same signed request, Live
opening included, again for up to five seconds within its deadline: a provider
reconnecting is briefly absent. A finite RPC is never sent, first or again,
after its deadline: a caller that reaches the send late gets the timeout error
and the service never receives that request. A Live opening follows the same
rule within the caller's timeout, so a late opening never reserves a provider
session for a caller that has given up. A no-responders failure after that
wait means the target service is not currently reachable; it is not a malformed
offer, a declared error, or a failed Operation. Providers in both SDKs accept
a request signed up to 30 seconds before they verify it, which includes time
spent queued behind the handler's earlier requests.

Declare expected RPC and Operation errors in IDL to obtain typed generated error
handling. Runtime validation and transport failures remain distinct from those
business errors. Declared constraints (`min_length`, `max`, `max_items`, ...)
are enforced by both SDKs: a provider rejects an RPC or Operation input that
violates them with `ValidationError` before the handler runs, and TypeScript
callers refuse to send one, so handlers need not re-check them. Cursor-paginated RPCs end only when `nextCursor` is absent, and
pagination does not generally promise a snapshot.

### Events

Event subjects include the encoded qualified API identity and unpadded base64url
parameter tokens derived from payload pointers; listeners match the generated
wildcard pattern, and the message proof binds the exact API, dotted event name,
and parameter count. Subscriptions verify original bytes and proof before
decoding. Core NATS delivery requires live publisher authority; durable delivery
uses trusted original publication time, not today's publisher-context expiry.
Consumer authority remains current. Durable names remain Trellis-owned. A normal
publish happens immediately; it is not a database commit fence.

Durable success is acknowledged only after the handler succeeds. Retryable
failure uses the declared backoff; final exhaustion leaves delivery
unacknowledged so Events captures the broker max-deliveries advisory into that
Consumer's DLQ. Consumers have local per-process concurrency. Consumer ownership
permits retained inspection and terminal replay reporting, not administrative
Replay/Dismiss. Manual replay uses the same handler with a fresh delivery
budget, does not rewind the original Consumer, and confirms `resolved` before
acknowledging success. DLQ and replay retain the original broker publication
time and resolve original bytes and `originalPublishedAt` through authenticated,
resource-scoped Events inspection, even after source expiry; publisher headers
and replay publication time never replace them. Delivery and application side
effects remain at least once.

### Live

Live observations and Operation watchers are authorized live sessions negotiated
with bounded opening requests. The provider signs its offer and frames; control
responses bind the session ID, logical command sequence, and command hash, and
continued authority is rechecked from retained context rather than a network
lookup per frame. Both SDKs verify the exact consumer binding in Live offers. A
session has protocol liveness and credit bounds, not a total age or message cap.
Closing returns a receipt whose remote-cleanup state is complete, incomplete, or
unconfirmed, and reconnect is an explicit new open rather than a silent reopen.

Live uses `trellis.live.v1` even for application APIs such as `documents@v2`.
Generated canonical opening subjects are
`live.v1.route.<b64(full_api_id)>.<action>`, with unpadded base64url identity
tokens. The application's major belongs to that full API identity, not the Live
protocol version. Use generated client/provider facades; dotted action names
never imply a deployment selection or another Live protocol.

### Operations

Operations are durable, restartable, at-least-once caller-visible workflows.
Their identity is `<API identity>@v<major>:operation:<action>` across SDKs,
storage, and complete references; generated aliases are not durable identities.
Canonical starts honor that API major, while owner-directed controls retain the
fixed `operation.v1` transport family. Implementation-only providers can forward
their own updates without receiving caller Observe authority. Transient updates
carry operationId, sequence, timestamp, the declared update, and the unchanged
observed snapshot.

Complete serialized references require `deploymentId`, checked against certified
signed acceptance. SDKs route get/watch/wait/cancel/signals to that deployment,
not an instance, and restore only complete references, never IDs alone. Replicas
in that deployment retain executor leases and CAS fencing. References are
routing metadata, not authority. A handler can read its own complete reference,
for example to put in a return URL it builds mid-operation; the caller resumes
with it, and only a caller allowed to observe the operation can. Invocation
deduplication is deployment-scoped:
never automatically retry an uncertain canonical start into another deployment;
no cross-deployment idempotency is promised.

Starts default to canonical routing. An explicit targeted start persists
deployment, invocation ULID, and frozen input before the first send and never
